topic: keeping a marsh wind pump at work: scoop wheel depth, a leaking sluice and how much cloth to set

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-5)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: rejestrator poziomu wody w rowie

base: I look after a small wind pump on the marsh and it lifts water far too slowly.
An old sluice at the far end of the dyke still holds back the tide well.
A depth logger stands in the dyke and marks the water height every hour.
The sails turn steadily in a good breeze, yet the scoop wheel barely moves water.
Should I look first at the sails, or at the gearing down in the pit?
Look at the scoop wheel first, because a wheel set too deep swallows all your power.
Depth of immersion decides everything, and a few inches too far is enough to stall it.
Measure how far the paddles enter the water when the wheel stands still.
Only then judge the sails, since they can do nothing about a drowned wheel.
The paddles enter nearly two feet, which sounds a great deal more than it should.
The depth logger shows the dyke has risen four inches since the autumn rain.
The old sluice may be letting a little water back at every high tide.
Do I raise the wheel, or bring the water down before anything else?
Bring the water down first, since raising a scoop wheel is heavy work in a pit.
Four inches on the dyke will drown any wheel set for a normal season.
Check the sluice doors on a falling tide and watch for water creeping back.
A door that fails to seat will undo a whole night of pumping by morning.
One sluice door had a baulk of timber jammed under it, holding it open.
We cleared it and the depth logger shows the dyke down five inches in two days.
The scoop wheel now turns freely and throws water properly at every revolution.
Should I still raise the wheel for the summer, or leave it where it sits?
Leave it, because a wheel set right for winter will manage the summer easily.
Summer water is low anyway and the pump has little to do until autumn.
Spend the quiet months on the sails and the brake, which both wear unseen.
Walk the sluice every month as well, since timber and weed collect there constantly.
I stripped the sails and found two of the cloth frames badly split at the heel.
The brake band is thin in one place and squeals whenever I set it hard.
The mill has stood idle for three weeks while I work through the repairs.
Which of the two should be finished first, and can the mill run meanwhile?
The brake comes first, always, because a mill you cannot stop is worth nothing.
Fit a new band and dress the wheel rim smooth before you touch the sails.
Two split frames will carry cloth for a season if you bind them with iron.
Run the mill on the two sound sails until the frames are properly rebuilt.
The new brake band is on and the mill stops cleanly from a good speed.
I ran it on two sails for a fortnight and the dyke held its level.
Both frames are rebuilt now and I hope to set full cloth next week.
How much cloth should go on in an ordinary autumn wind off the sea?
In an ordinary breeze, sword point is plenty and leaves you room to shorten.
Full cloth belongs to light airs only, whatever the old millers used to boast.
A marsh wind rises fast and you cannot always get up to take cloth off.
Set less than you think and let the mill run all night without worry.
